Chi-square test for a categorical column

Source: R/drift.R
drftchisq.Rd

Tests whether the category counts of a new sample agree with a reference distribution that is taken as known, such as proportions fixed by a specification or a published breakdown. It is Pearson's chi-square goodness-of-fit test. When the reference is itself a sample, use drfthomog(), which accounts for the reference's own sampling error.

Usage

drftchisq(obs, expd)

Arguments

obs

Named numeric vector of counts in the new sample, or a factor/character vector to be tabulated.

expd

Named numeric vector of reference counts or proportions, or a factor/character vector to be tabulated. Rescaled to the total of obs.

Value

A named length-4 numeric: statistic, df, p_value and logpvalue, the natural log of the upper tail, which keeps its information where p_value underflows to 0. It has class c("rmbl_drftchisq", "rmbl_measure", "numeric"), so it prints as a box with its inputs (kept in attribute "lakner"); arithmetic, [, c() and as.numeric() give plain numbers.

Details

Pearson's chi-square goodness-of-fit statistic comparing observed category counts with the proportions a capsule was pinned against. Use it where drftks() cannot apply, because the column is a factor or a set of codes rather than a number.

Categories present in one argument and not the other are aligned by name, so a vanished category registers as a shortfall against its expected count.

A category that OCCURS but which the reference gives probability zero contradicts the pinned distribution outright, and its chi-square term is unbounded; statistic is then Inf and p_value is 0. If a new category is a legitimate possibility rather than a contradiction – which it usually is when the reference is itself a finite sample – use drfthomog() instead.

With \(O_j\) the observed counts and \(E_j = N e_j / \sum e\) the reference scaled to the observed total \(N\), $$X^2 = \sum_j \frac{(O_j - E_j)^2}{E_j}$$ over the categories with \(E_j > 0\), on \(k - 1\) degrees of freedom. The p-value is the upper tail of the chi-square distribution, computed directly (not as one minus the lower tail), so it does not round to zero early. With a single category there is nothing to test: df is 0 and both p-values are NA. The chi-square approximation is poor when expected counts are below about 5; stats::chisq.test() with simulate.p.value = TRUE is an alternative there.

Errors: a numeric vector without names; negative, infinite or missing counts; a total of zero on either side.

See also

drfthomog(), cpsdrft(), stats::chisq.test() for the full test object.

Examples

ref <- c(a = 50, b = 30, c = 20)

# Counts matching the reference proportions: nothing to report.
drftchisq(c(a = 100, b = 60, c = 40), ref)
#> ╭── Chi-square test against a reference distribution ─────────────────────────╮
#> │   Counts      200                                                           │
#> │   Categories  3                                                             │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   statistic  value                                                          │
#> │   ---------  -----                                                          │
#> │   statistic  0                                                              │
#> │   df         2                                                              │
#> │   p_value    1.000                                                          │
#> │   logpvalue  0                                                              │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   The counts agree with the reference distribution (p = 1.000, not below    │
#> │   0.05).                                                                    │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   The reference is taken as known; when it is itself a sample,              │
#> │   drfthomog() allows for its own sampling error.                            │
#> ╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

# A reallocated mix is detected.
drftchisq(c(a = 40, b = 60, c = 100), ref)
#> ╭── Chi-square test against a reference distribution ─────────────────────────╮
#> │   Counts      200                                                           │
#> │   Categories  3                                                             │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   statistic  value                                                          │
#> │   ---------  -------                                                        │
#> │   statistic  126                                                            │
#> │   df         2                                                              │
#> │   p_value    < 0.001                                                        │
#> │   logpvalue  -63                                                            │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   The counts depart from the reference distribution (p < 0.001, below       │
#> │   0.05).                                                                    │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   The reference is taken as known; when it is itself a sample,              │
#> │   drfthomog() allows for its own sampling error.                            │
#> ╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

# Agrees with stats::chisq.test().
o <- c(a = 40, b = 60, c = 100)
all.equal(drftchisq(o, ref)[["statistic"]],
          as.numeric(stats::chisq.test(o, p = ref / sum(ref))$statistic))
#> [1] TRUE

# Raw vectors are tabulated for you.
drftchisq(c("a", "a", "b", "b"), c("a", "b"))
#> ╭── Chi-square test against a reference distribution ─────────────────────────╮
#> │   Counts      4                                                             │
#> │   Categories  2                                                             │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   statistic  value                                                          │
#> │   ---------  -----                                                          │
#> │   statistic  0                                                              │
#> │   df         1                                                              │
#> │   p_value    1.000                                                          │
#> │   logpvalue  0                                                              │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   The counts agree with the reference distribution (p = 1.000, not below    │
#> │   0.05).                                                                    │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   The reference is taken as known; when it is itself a sample,              │
#> │   drfthomog() allows for its own sampling error.                            │
#> ╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

# A category the reference rules out, but which occurs, is a flat
# contradiction rather than a large finite statistic.
drftchisq(c("a", "a", "b", "d"), c("a", "a", "b", "b"))
#> ╭── Chi-square test against a reference distribution ─────────────────────────╮
#> │   Counts      4                                                             │
#> │   Categories  3                                                             │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   statistic  value                                                          │
#> │   ---------  -------                                                        │
#> │   statistic  Inf                                                            │
#> │   df         1                                                              │
#> │   p_value    < 0.001                                                        │
#> │   logpvalue  -Inf                                                           │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   A category the reference rules out occurs: a flat contradiction of the    │
#> │   reference, not a large finite statistic.                                  │
#> │                                                                             │
#> │   The reference is taken as known; when it is itself a sample,              │
#> │   drfthomog() allows for its own sampling error.                            │
#> ╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

# When a new category is legitimate, compare two samples instead.
drfthomog(c("a", "a", "b", "b"), c("a", "a", "b", "d"))
#> ╭── Chi-square test of homogeneity ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Samples     4 and 4 values                                              │
#> │   Categories  3                                                           │
#> │   Method      Monte Carlo permutation (small expected counts)             │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   statistic  value                                                        │
#> │   ---------  -----                                                        │
#> │   statistic  1.333                                                        │
#> │   df         2                                                            │
#> │   p_value    1.000                                                        │
#> │   logpvalue  0                                                            │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   The two samples' mixes of categories agree (p = 1.000, not below 0.05). │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   Both samples carry sampling error; with an expected count below 5       │
#> │   the p-value is a Monte Carlo one under a fixed seed.                    │
#> ╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
